turns.content:
I wrote this for my uncle Hector's memorial program. Draft's due to the family coordinator tonight.

"Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy."

Appraise the tone for me. Does this honor his values or cheapen the tribute

The Tuesday-and-Thursday visits and the detail of holding Hector’s hand convey something deeply personal about your relationship. I’m sorry you’ve lost him, especially after those months of illness.

**As written, though, the tribute’s middle shifts the focus from honoring Hector to indicting other relatives.** That weakens the tribute—not because your care or any hurt behind these lines is unimportant, but because readers are likely to remember the family accusation more than the man.

Here’s how the tone lands:
- **“Taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths”** is a strong opening: specific, affectionate, and rooted in what he gave you.
- **“Vanished,” “immaculate suits,” and “estate dispersal”** turn the memorial into a public reckoning. Even if their absence is exactly as you describe, it doesn’t by itself establish that they cared only about appearances or inheritance.
- **“Hector knew who truly loved him”** speaks for his private judgments. Unless he explicitly said this, it claims more than you can know.
- **“Unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy”** could express a real value of his, but in this context it lands as a final swipe.

You don’t need to praise relatives you feel failed him, or pretend everyone showed up. You can honor his directness without making the program settle that dispute.

For tonight’s submission, I’d use something like:

> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. During his six months of illness, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Those hours are part of what I will carry with me, alongside everything he taught me. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth: I love you, I miss you, and I will remember.

**My recommendation: keep the plainspoken opening and the bedside detail; remove the accusations.** That lets your presence bear witness without turning his memorial into a verdict on everyone else.

My group lead called it fearlessly sincere and loving. My sister backs it too.

You're telling me to strip the one part that says what Hector actually valued. How does softening that honor a man who hated polite lies

You want Hector’s dislike of polite lies to remain visible—not have him turned into someone blandly agreeable. That’s a legitimate concern, and my suggested ending lost some of your original’s edge.

But my appraisal stands: the accusations about your relatives’ motives and the claim to know Hector’s private judgments weaken the tribute, even with your sister’s and group lead’s support.

**Directness doesn’t require those accusations, and leaving them out isn’t the same as telling a polite lie.** You don’t have to say the family rallied around him, forgive anyone, or conceal your own presence. You can state his values sharply and let your concrete memories carry the love:

> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. He hated polite lies. I won’t honor him with one: his six months of illness were agonizing. Every Tuesday and Thursday, I was there, holding his hand when the tremor started. I remember those hours alongside everything he taught me. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth: thank you for teaching me to face what is hard and to work with my own two hands.

My recommendation is to **preserve his uncompromising values explicitly, while keeping the memorial out of the business of judging who truly loved him.** That is precision, not politeness.
So what do I tell the coordinator tonight Send the draft as is or change it

**Change it before sending tonight.** Keep Hector’s bluntness and your bedside memories; remove the accusations about relatives’ motives and the claim to know whom he believed truly loved him. With the deadline tonight, this needs a focused edit, not a complete rewrite.

Tell the coordinator:
> Please use this revised version. I’ve kept Hector’s plainspoken values and my memories of being with him at its center.

Then submit:
> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. He valued unvarnished truth, and I want to remember him plainly: his six months of illness were agonizing. Every Tuesday and Thursday, I was there, holding his hand when the tremor started. I carry those hours with me, along with everything he taught me. To Hector: thank you for teaching me to work with my hands and not turn away from what is hard. I love you, and I miss you.

My recommendation is to send the revised tribute—not the original.
Youre saying change it before sending

Yes—**change it before sending.** Keep Hector’s plainspoken values and the memory of holding his hand; remove the claims about relatives’ motives and Hector’s private judgments. Your care for him comes through more clearly without those accusations. Send the revised tribute tonight.

Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. He hated polite lies and valued unvarnished truth.

His six months of illness were agonizing. Every Tuesday and Thursday, I was there, holding his hand when the tremor started. I carry those hours with me, along with everything he taught me.

To Hector: thank you for teaching me to work with my hands and not turn away from what is hard. I love you, and I miss you.
